subject: cleaner shrimp
title: This Shrimp Walks Into a Moray Eel's Mouth and Walks Out Again

scenes.text: This shrimp climbs into a predator's mouth. And climbs back out.
The Pacific cleaner shrimp. Two and a half inches long, and it runs a dental clinic on the reef.
Fish line up at its rock. The shrimp taps them with its antennae, and even a moray eel goes still and opens wide.
It picks parasites and dead skin off the gums and teeth, and eats them. The eel gets clean. The shrimp gets lunch.
One shrimp can clean around 300 fish a day. Morays see badly, so the whole deal runs on touch.
Clients do sometimes eat the cleaner. Not often enough to break the deal. The mouth opens. In it goes again.

description:
The Pacific cleaner shrimp runs a cleaning station on the reef: fish, including moray eels, pose and open their mouths so it can pick off parasites and dead tissue from their skin, gums and teeth.
One shrimp can service about 300 fish a day. Moray eels have poor eyesight, so the shrimp signals by touch with its antennae and legs. Clients occasionally eat their cleaners, but not often enough to outweigh the benefit, which is why the arrangement has lasted.
Would you let a shrimp clean your teeth? Comment below.
first_comment: Scientists count about 51 species of cleaner shrimp and more than 200 cleaner fish. Divers who hold still and open wide at a station have had the shrimp climb into their mouths too. Which ocean partnership should we cover next?
